body:
What was the Delhi Sultanate?

The Delhi Sultanate was a succession of ruling dynasties that governed Delhi and extensive parts of the Indian subcontinent between 1206 and 1526. Its rulers were called Sultans. They maintained armies, appointed officials, collected revenue and attempted to extend their authority over distant territories.

Delhi had already become an important commercial centre under the Tomaras and Chauhans during the 12th century. The establishment of the Sultanate transformed it into the centre of a much larger political system. However, the territory actually controlled from Delhi changed considerably from one reign to another.

The 5 ruling dynasties

DynastyPeriodImportant rulers
Early Turkish rulers, commonly called the Mamluk or Slave dynasty1206–1290Qutbuddin Aibak, Iltutmish, Raziyya, Balban
Khalji1290–1320Jalaluddin Khalji, Alauddin Khalji
Tughluq1320–1414Ghiyasuddin Tughluq, Muhammad bin Tughluq, Firuz Shah Tughluq
Sayyid1414–1451Khizr Khan
Lodi1451–1526Bahlul Lodi, Sikandar Lodi, Ibrahim Lodi

The Sultanate began with Qutbuddin Aibak in 1206 and ended when Ibrahim Lodi was defeated by Babur in the First Battle of Panipat in 1526. The dynastic sequence provides the chronological framework for understanding administrative developments.

How the Sultan exercised authority

The Sultan stood at the centre of the administration. He appointed high officials, distributed revenue assignments, commanded military campaigns and exercised authority over taxation and justice. In practice, his power depended on the cooperation of nobles, governors, soldiers and local landholders.

Two traditional signs of sovereignty were sikka, the issuing of coins in the ruler's name, and khutba, the mention of the ruler in the Friday congregational sermon. These expressed claims to legitimate authority, although their use did not guarantee effective control over every locality.

Persian was the language of administration. Historical accounts written in Persian were called tarikh in the singular and tawarikh in the plural. They provide information about rulers and governance, but many were composed by courtiers who expected royal patronage.

Why agriculture and the army were connected

A large army required regular supplies and salaries. These expenses depended heavily on revenue collected from cultivators. Successful cultivation, therefore, supported the financial and military strength of the state.

The 13th-century writer Fakhr-i Mudabbir described this interdependence through the idea of a circle of justice: good government helped cultivators prosper; prosperous cultivators could pay revenue; revenue supported soldiers; and soldiers helped maintain the ruler's authority.

This was an ideal of governance rather than proof that every Sultan ruled justly. High taxation, warfare and disputes with local chiefs could damage agricultural production and weaken the state.

Prelims focus

  • The Delhi Sultanate lasted from 1206 to 1526.
  • The dynastic order was Early Turkish, Khalji, Tughluq, Sayyid and Lodi.
  • Persian was the language of Sultanate administration.
  • Tarikh is singular; tawarikh is plural.
  • Fakhr-i Mudabbir explained the interdependence of justice, cultivators, revenue and soldiers.
  • Trap: A Sultan's claim to authority over a territory did not always mean that Delhi exercised effective control there.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 3, The Delhi Sultans, printed pp. 30–36, 2020–21 edition; IGNOU, eGyanKosh, Indian Polity: The Sultanate, Unit 16, Administration of the Sultanate, sections on kingship and central administration, consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: The Delhi Sultanate: Political Authority and Administrative Foundations

body:
The Sultan could not govern alone

Territorial expansion created a need for officials who could manage revenue, armies, correspondence and provincial administration. The Delhi Sultans developed central departments to carry out these functions, although their organisation and importance varied between reigns.

Principal departments and officials

Department or officePrincipal functionAssociated official
Diwan-i-WizaratFinance, revenue accounts and expenditureWazir
Diwan-i-ArzMilitary administration, inspection and organisationAriz-i-Mumalik
Diwan-i-InshaRoyal correspondence and official ordersSenior secretarial officials

The wazir supervised important financial matters, including the state's income and expenditure. The ariz-i-mumalik was concerned with military administration. This officer was not necessarily the commander of every army in battle; military command remained dependent on the Sultan and the commanders he appointed.

Reports from officials, couriers and intelligence agents helped the ruler obtain information about provincial conditions. A royal order was useful only when officials and local authorities were willing and able to implement it.

Who were the nobles?

The nobility consisted of influential military and administrative elites who served the Sultan. Nobles could command troops, govern territories and exercise considerable influence at court. Many depended on the ruler for offices and revenue assignments, but powerful nobles could also challenge a weak Sultan.

Bandagan: trained military slaves

The early Sultans, particularly Iltutmish, appointed specially trained slaves known in Persian as bandagan. Some were purchased for military service, trained in warfare and administration, and promoted to important positions.

The political advantage for the Sultan was personal dependence: a trained officer who owed his advancement to the ruler might be more trustworthy than an established landed chief with an independent power base.

These elite military slaves must be distinguished from the much larger population of enslaved people employed in domestic service, workshops and other occupations. Promotion to high office was possible for selected individuals, not an opportunity available equally to all enslaved people.

Clients and people of humble origin

The Khalji and Tughluq rulers also appointed clients and individuals from less privileged backgrounds to important positions. A client was a dependent who received protection and advancement from a powerful patron.

During the reign of Muhammad bin Tughluq, appointments of people from occupational backgrounds outside the established nobility attracted criticism from the chronicler Ziyauddin Barani. His criticism reflected the social prejudices of an elite writer; it does not establish that such appointees were necessarily incapable administrators.

Why succession caused conflicts among nobles

Personal loyalty could create a serious problem when a Sultan died. Officers promoted by the former ruler might not support his successor. The new Sultan might appoint his own dependants, producing rivalry between older and newer groups of nobles.

The reign of Raziyya (1236–1240), Iltutmish's daughter, illustrates another aspect of noble power. She became Sultan, but influential nobles resisted her attempts to govern independently. Her removal in 1240 also reflected contemporary gender prejudices against female rule.

Political distinction: A person could be a powerful officer because of royal appointment rather than hereditary landownership. Nevertheless, such an officer could acquire enough military and political influence to oppose the Sultan.

Prelims focus

  • Wazir: principal financial administrator.
  • Diwan-i-Arz: department of military administration.
  • Diwan-i-Insha: department of official correspondence.
  • Bandagan: specially trained slaves who could receive important military and administrative appointments.
  • Iltutmish relied heavily on trained military slaves.
  • Trap: An elite bandagan serving as a governor was not representative of every enslaved person in Sultanate society.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 3, The Delhi Sultans, printed pp. 32–38, 2020–21 edition; IGNOU, eGyanKosh, Indian Polity: The Sultanate, Unit 16, Administration of the Sultanate, sections on central departments and officials, consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: Central Administration, Nobility and Political Loyalty

body:
Meaning of iqta

An iqta was a territorial revenue assignment granted by the Sultan to an official, commonly in return for military and administrative service. Its holder was known as an iqtadar or muqti.

The iqta system helped the Sultanate administer territories without paying every provincial commander directly from the treasury at Delhi. An appointed commander could meet authorised expenses from the revenue of the area assigned to him.

An iqta was not automatically the private property of its holder. The Sultan retained the authority to appoint, transfer or remove the official. The distinction between an assignment of revenue and ownership of land is essential for understanding the system.

Duties of the muqti

The muqti combined military and administrative responsibilities. His principal duties included:

  • Leading military campaigns when ordered by the Sultan.
  • Maintaining law and order within the assigned territory.
  • Collecting the revenue authorised by the state.
  • Maintaining the required soldiers and meeting their expenses from the permitted revenue.
  • Remitting any revenue surplus due to the central treasury under the applicable arrangement.

For example, if a muqti received an assignment in a district, he could collect the prescribed revenue and use the authorised portion for his remuneration and the soldiers he maintained. This did not entitle him to impose unlimited taxes or pass the territory permanently to his children.

How the centre tried to control muqtis

An influential governor might gradually behave as an independent ruler. To prevent this, the Sultans attempted to keep the office transferable and non-hereditary. They could move a muqti from one assignment to another, reducing the chance that he would create a permanent local power base.

Under Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad bin Tughluq, transfers and financial scrutiny were enforced particularly strongly. State-appointed accountants examined collections and expenditure. Officials were expected to verify that the muqti maintained the required number of soldiers.

The surplus remaining after authorised expenses was generally referred to as fawazil and could be demanded by the central government. The effectiveness of such supervision differed according to the ruler and region.

Iqta, khalisa and kharaj are different concepts

TermMeaningMain distinction
IqtaTerritorial revenue assignmentConnected to an official's service and expenses
KhalisaLand or territory whose revenue was reserved directly for the central treasuryRevenue was not assigned as an iqta
KharajLand revenue or tax on cultivationA type of tax, not an administrative territory

Thus, a question asking about kharaj concerns taxation, whereas a question asking about the muqti concerns a revenue-assignment holder with military and administrative duties.

Why distant provinces were difficult to control

Delhi's authority was strongest where the government could move troops, supervise officials and collect revenue regularly. Distant provinces could become difficult to manage because of slow communication, local resistance and competing military powers.

Bengal repeatedly presented problems of effective control from Delhi. In southern India, military victories did not guarantee lasting political authority, and several territories subsequently emerged as independent states. Even closer to Delhi, forested and mountainous regions could remain under local chiefs.

Under Firuz Shah Tughluq, hereditary claims to offices and assignments received greater acceptance than under some earlier rulers. Therefore, the principle of non-hereditary assignment must not be mistaken for an unchanging rule throughout the Sultanate.

Prelims focus

  • Iqta: territorial revenue assignment.
  • Muqti or iqtadar: holder of an iqta.
  • Muqtis maintained troops, led campaigns and maintained order.
  • Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad bin Tughluq enforced transfers and closer supervision of muqtis.
  • Khalisa: revenue reserved directly for the central government.
  • Trap: An iqta was not necessarily hereditary private landownership.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 3, The Delhi Sultans, printed pp. 38–40, 2020–21 edition; IGNOU, eGyanKosh, Indian Polity: The Sultanate, Unit 16, sections on provincial administration and the iqta system, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: How an iqta connected provincial revenue to military service and central supervision.

title: The Iqta System and Relations Between Delhi and the Provinces

body:
Why land revenue mattered

Agriculture supported the greater part of the population during the Sultanate period. It also supplied the revenue that financed armies, court expenditure and administration. The state therefore sought regular control over cultivated land and its produce.

A tax could be collected directly by state officials or through authorised intermediaries and provincial revenue assignees. The method of assessment and the actual burden on peasants varied between regions and rulers.

Important revenue terms

TermWhat it concernedExam distinction
KharajCultivation or agricultural land revenuePrincipal agrarian tax
CharaiGrazing or cattleNot a tax on houses
GhariHousesNot a tax on crops
JizyaPoll tax on non-Muslim subjects, generally adult males; women and children were exemptDistinct from land revenue

Other fiscal terms included zakat, obligatory alms on eligible Muslim-owned wealth (normally 2.5% on monetary wealth held at or above the minimum taxable amount, or nisab, for 1 lunar year), and khums, associated with a prescribed 1/5 share of certain war booty and other specified receipts. Their collection and treatment by rulers varied over time. They should not be confused with the ordinary assessment of cultivated land.

Alauddin Khalji's revenue measures

Alauddin Khalji attempted to bring land assessment and revenue collection more firmly under direct state control. His administrators measured cultivated land and maintained accounts. In important areas under his direct authority, the agricultural demand was assessed at approximately 50% of the produce.

The 50% figure is associated particularly with Alauddin's measures in the territories where they were implemented. It must not be treated as the uniform land revenue rate for every Sultan, province or century.

The reform also restricted the traditional rights of powerful local chiefs to collect additional taxes. Wealthy landlords and chiefs could themselves be made liable to pay the prescribed revenue.

Local intermediaries and village administration

Although the central government wanted control over revenue, it depended on people who understood village boundaries, crops and local households. Important intermediaries included:

  • Muqaddam: village headman involved in local administration and revenue collection.
  • Khut or khot: a local headman or privileged rural intermediary in parts of northern India.
  • Chaudhuri: an intermediary associated with revenue administration over a wider group of villages or localities.
  • Record-keeping officials: personnel responsible for accounts, assessments and information about holdings.

These terms did not always describe identical offices throughout the subcontinent. Their importance lay in the connection they provided between cultivators and the state.

How revenue affected cultivation

The state required grain and money, but peasants also needed seed, food and resources for the next agricultural season. Heavy or poorly timed taxation could reduce their ability to continue cultivation, especially during drought or famine.

Revenue collected in grain could supply soldiers and city markets, while cash collections helped finance salaries and other purchases. This connected village production directly to the military and urban economy.

Keep the qualification: About 50% of produce was the assessment associated with Alauddin Khalji's revenue reforms in important controlled territories. It is not a timeless definition of kharaj.

Prelims focus

  • Kharaj: land revenue or tax on cultivation.
  • Charai: tax associated with cattle or grazing.
  • Ghari: house tax.
  • Alauddin Khalji strengthened state assessment through land measurement and revenue records.
  • The agricultural demand under his reforms was about 50% of produce in the relevant territories.
  • Trap: Jizya and kharaj were different fiscal categories.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 3, The Delhi Sultans, printed p. 39, 2020–21 edition; NCERT, Delhi: 12th to 15th Century, Class 7, Chapter 3, printed pp. 34–35, 2024–25 reprint; IGNOU, eGyanKosh, Economy of the Delhi Sultanate, Units 19–20, sections on state revenue and agrarian structure, consulted 19 November 2026.]
